title: The Righteous
hookLine: non-Jews who risked their lives to hide and save Jews
carry: someone knocked, you open the door

lines: A DOOR THAT COULD COST EVERYTHING.
cards: A tree on a hillside in Jerusalem, with a small plaque at its foot. On the plaque, a name that isn't Jewish: a farmer's, perhaps, or a nun's, or a diplomat's. Walk a little further and there's another tree, another name.

Each marks someone who was not Jewish, who lived through the Nazi years, and who hid a Jewish neighbor in an attic, forged a paper, or opened a door when opening it could have cost everything. Some were caught.
Some were never thanked in their lifetimes. Today, the title they were given.

teach.b: Yad Vashem, Israel's Holocaust memorial, gives these people a title: Righteous Among the Nations. In Hebrew, chasidei umot ha-olam. The idea is much older than the war.

A rabbinic teaching in the Tosefta says the righteous of the nations of the world have a share in the world to come. Goodness, in that teaching, doesn't belong to one people. The stories are as different as the people.
André and Magda Trocmé, a pastor and his wife in the French village of Le Chambon-sur-Lignon, where villagers took in Jewish children and refugees.
Chiune Sugihara, a Japanese diplomat in Lithuania, who kept writing transit visas after his government had said no.

teach.h: A VILLAGE, A DIPLOMAT, A SOCIAL WORKER.
teach.b: Irena Sendler, a social worker in Warsaw, who helped smuggle children out of the ghetto. And people whose names are known only to the families they hid, or to no one at all.
Asked later why they did it, some rescuers gave answers so plain they sound almost like a shrug.

teach.h: SOMEONE KNOCKED. YOU OPEN THE DOOR.
teach.b: Someone knocked. You open the door.
The book of Proverbs asks the same of its reader: rescue those being dragged toward death, and don't hold back. No one, it adds, can excuse themselves by saying they didn't know.
Remembering the righteous doesn't soften the history around them. It shows something harder: even then, a person could still choose.

how: Jewish communities honor rescuers through Yad Vashem's title Righteous Among the Nations, with trees and names at the memorial in Jerusalem; some families stay in touch with the families of those who hid them.

games.q: you live in an occupied town. late at night, someone knocks: a Jewish family with nowhere to hide. what do you do?
games.why: the righteous opened the door. asked why, some gave answers as plain as a shrug: someone knocked.

practice: Bring to mind one person who once took a risk on your behalf, and small counts: a teacher who stood up for you, a friend who told you a hard truth, a stranger who stopped when others walked past.
Let their face come clear, and notice what the risk might have cost them. If you pray, give thanks for them in the words of your own tradition; if not, simply hold them in mind with gratitude.

wordCard.voice: The Righteous. In full, the Righteous Among the Nations: people who were not Jewish and risked their lives to hide and save Jews.

orig.note: Hebrew: the pious ones of the nations of the world, the title Yad Vashem gives rescuers.

carryVoice: Your line: someone knocked, you open the door. A plain answer, and a life behind it. Back tomorrow, same hill.
